name: PF-06260414

lead: PF-06260414 is an oral SARM from Pfizer, studied for cachexia, which muscle-building readers follow as a lean-mass candidate.

It belongs to the isoquinoline class and is designed to activate androgen receptors preferentially in muscle and bone. A 2016 paper reported tolerability, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic results from single and multiple ascending oral doses in healthy men. Development was discontinued after Phase I, and efficacy was never tested in trials.

paras: It was given orally in a clinical setting. It is not marketed, and no routine for physique use exists.
Only Phase I tolerability data exist. The SARM class is unapproved and banned by WADA, with case reports of liver injury from recreational use.

angle.text: PF-06260414 is Pfizer's oral SARM, studied for cachexia and designed to activate androgen receptors in muscle and bone. Muscle-building readers follow it as a lean-mass candidate. It was safety-tested in healthy men and shelved after Phase I, with no appearance data.

lead: PF-06260414 is an investigational non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) of the isoquinoline class, developed by Pfizer. It was investigated for muscle-wasting conditions such as cachexia and for androgen replacement, and development was discontinued after Phase I [1][2].

The appeal of SARMs for physique is that they are designed to activate androgen receptors preferentially in muscle and bone, which is the pathway through which anabolic hormones build lean mass; in the chain people describe, activating those receptors could mean more lean mass and a more muscular look. For PF-06260414 specifically, that chain has not been tested: the published work is a Phase I safety and pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers [2].

The compound is better known to researchers than to the public. It appears in a class-wide systematic review of SARM trials [3] and in several doping-control analytical papers that include it among SARMs that testing laboratories screen for [4][5][6][7].

paras: PF-06260414 is a non-steroidal small molecule with the formula C14H14N4O2S and a molar mass of about 302 g/mol. Its systematic name describes an isoquinoline-1-carbonitrile bearing a cyclic sulfonamide (thiadiazinane dioxide) group [8]. Unlike anabolic-androgenic steroids it has no steroid backbone, which is the defining feature of the SARM class [1].

As a SARM it targets the androgen receptor, with the stated aim of tissue-selective effects: anabolic action in muscle and bone with less stimulation of tissues such as prostate [1][8]. In the Phase I study, hormones of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis were measured to characterise its pharmacodynamics, and the authors reported HPG axis modulation in both Western and Japanese participants [2].

After oral administration the compound was absorbed quickly, with a median time to peak concentration of about one to two hours and a half-life of roughly 7 to 13 hours. Exposure was dose-proportional and time-independent. Peak and overall exposure in Japanese participants were higher than in Western participants (98.6 percent higher Cmax and 79.5 percent higher AUC), with similar effects on the HPG axis [2].

Pfizer's programme produced two Phase I registrations. A single and multiple ascending dose study in 72 healthy Western and Japanese men started in February 2014 and is listed as completed [9]. A 2015 relative bioavailability study comparing a spray-dried solid dose with a suspension formulation was registered and then withdrawn [10]. No later phases are recorded, and Wikipedia lists the compound as an investigational new drug in the United States [8].

In the Phase I study there were no serious adverse events. The most frequent were increases in the liver enzyme alanine aminotransferase (seven subjects) and headache (three subjects) [2]. Liver injury has also been reported in case reports for other SARMs used outside trials, according to class-level summaries [1].

SARMs as a class are unapproved and are on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list, and doping laboratories have developed methods to detect them in human, equine and bovine samples. PF-06260414 is included in several such panels: a mass-spectrometry study characterised its fragmentation pattern [4], an equine liver microsome study identified its metabolites [5], a UHPLC-MS/MS method for blood in horses and cattle includes it with a detection capability of 1 ng/mL [6], and a stability study covers 15 SARM compounds in urine and solvent [7]. These papers describe suspected and repeatedly documented SARM misuse in amateur and elite sport and the risk to animal-derived food [4][6].

A 2025 systematic review of randomized trials examined SARMs' effects on physical performance and safety across the class [3]. Analytical chemistry papers cover SARMs, including mass spectrometry and doping-control methods [4][5][6].

The Phase I trial (NCT02070939; published 2016 in Clinical Therapeutics) was a randomised, ascending-dose study in healthy subjects. Cohorts of eight received single or multiple oral doses across a wide range, with additional cohorts for once-daily dosing and a Japanese group of seven. Outcomes were tolerability, pharmacokinetics and HPG-axis hormones. The drug was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events [2][9].

A systematic review of nine randomized studies (970 patients, mean age 57.1 years, mean follow-up 80 days) covered six SARMs including PF-06260414, and evaluated stair-climbing power, leg press strength, lean body mass and fat mass along with safety across the class [3]. A follow-up bioavailability study was withdrawn [10]. No efficacy trial of PF-06260414 alone has been reported.
